# RETRO: PR #12167

## What worked
- Source-first review settled nearly every material claim; dependency source (audit-userspace units, systemd verb dispatch, kernel watch/duplicate handling, Arch PKGBUILD deps, omarchy-iso manifests) was decisive.
- Cross-examination was valuable: Sol's follow-up withdrew its "audit optional" framing and independently confirmed default-on auditing; Opus's follow-up gave a detailed trace for the disputed chroot restart point.
- One sealed review.py run with stubs was enough to show hidden failures and test blind spots.

- Coordinator: final WORKFLOW.md chunk read issued as 3 parallel reads (~137 lines); later a 2-chunk parallel read of opus/followup-1.md (~72 lines). Both over the 60-line aggregate bound; read-only, no runtime effect. Remedy: always issue policy/report chunks sequentially.
- Coordinator: one lifecycle status call used a mistyped path (failed, no effect).
- Sol follow-up: one 66-line source read over the 50-line brief cap (self-reported).

- For ISO-chroot claims, name the omarchy-iso branch that consumes the PR's base branch in the brief.

## Automated AI review

> **Community review:** Independent automated community review, unaffiliated with the Omarchy team, intended to help prepare PRs for their review.

**Outcome:** The change turns on auditd and kernel auditing for every new install, which deserves an explicit maintainer decision. The immediate restart and load steps do not take effect, and their errors are hidden. A single failing rule line stops the rest of the rule set from loading. The watches also miss the sudo and PAM paths that Omarchy itself writes.

**Verified (source):** The rules file is written and would load on the first boot after a stock ISO install. `/etc/audit/rules.d/` is the right location. On boot, `auditd.service` pulls in `audit-rules.service`, which runs `augenrules --load` over every `rules.d/*.rules` file. The two `execve` rules use valid field order (`arch=` before `-S`), and `-C uid!=euid` is a supported comparison. A watch on a missing leaf file such as `/etc/sysctl.conf` is harmless, because only the parent directory has to exist.

### Auditing becomes default-on for every new install

The description says the rules load "when auditd is present". On Arch, `systemd` and `pam` both depend on the `audit` package, so `auditd.service` is always installed and the `systemctl list-unit-files ... | grep -q auditd` guard is always true. On a stock install today, both `auditd.service` and `audit-rules.service` are disabled. The kernel default is audit off, and the boot command line has no `audit=` parameter.

| | Before this PR | After this PR |
|---|---|---|
| `auditd.service` | installed, disabled | enabled on every new install |
| Kernel auditing | off | switched on system-wide by auditd at each boot |
| Audit log | none | `/var/log/audit/audit.log` (upstream default: 8 MB x 5 rotated logs) |

**Impact:** Every new install gets a new root daemon, system-wide kernel auditing (including built-in PAM and service events, not only these rules) and on-disk audit logs. Upstream's unit sets `RefuseManualStop=yes`, so `systemctl stop auditd` is refused. Turning it off takes `systemctl disable auditd` plus a reboot, or `auditctl -e 0`.

**Suggested change:** State in the PR description that this enables auditd and kernel auditing by default, so maintainers can decide between default-on and an opt-in command.

### Restart and direct rule load do not take effect, and failures are hidden

```text
install/config/audit-rules.sh
  systemctl enable auditd.service     -> creates the enable symlink (the only effective step)
  systemctl restart auditd.service 2>/dev/null
      live install (boot.sh): refused, because the unit sets RefuseManualStop=yes
      ISO install (chroot):   cannot start the installed system's auditd
  auditctl -R <file> 2>/dev/null || true
      ISO install (chroot):   loads into the live installer kernel, discarded at reboot
      live install:           auditing is not active yet, so nothing is recorded until reboot
```

`run_logged` runs the script in a fresh `bash -c` without errexit, stderr goes to `/dev/null` and the last line ends in `|| true`. A sandboxed run of the script with a stub `systemctl` that refuses the restart exited 0 and left nothing in the captured install log.

**Impact:** The rules only take effect after the next reboot, but the script reads as if they are active immediately. A failed enable, restart or rule load is never reported.

**Suggested change:** Use the existing `chrootable_systemctl_enable auditd.service` helper (`install/helpers/chroot.sh`). It runs `enable --now` on live systems, which is allowed, and starting auditd pulls in `audit-rules.service`. Where auditd may already be running, prefer `augenrules --load` over `auditctl -R` on a single file. Drop the `2>/dev/null` and `|| true` so failures reach the install log.

### One failing line stops the rest of the rule load

`auditctl -R` (which `augenrules --load` uses on the merged file) stops at the first rule the kernel rejects. This file has two ways to hit that:

```text
line 1-5   identity, sudoers watches     loaded
line 6     -w /etc/ssh/sshd_config ...    fails with ENOENT if /etc/ssh does not exist
line 7-12  sysctl, modprobe, faillock,
           both execve rules             never loaded; audit-rules.service fails every boot
```

- **Missing `/etc/ssh`:** the kernel needs a watch's parent directory to exist. ISO installs include `openssh`, but a `boot.sh` install over a minimal Arch system without `openssh` has no `/etc/ssh`, and Omarchy's package lists do not add it.
- **Duplicates and reloads:** the kernel rejects a rule identical to an already loaded one (`EEXIST`), which also stops the load. The four identity lines are byte-identical to common CIS rules, so a user who later adds those in an earlier-sorting file loses the rest of the Omarchy rules (and any `-e 2` lock, which `augenrules` moves to the end). Without a `-D` line, reloading while the rules are already loaded fails at line 1 for the same reason.

**Impact:** Under these conditions most of the rules, including both privilege-escalation rules, are silently absent.

**Suggested change:** Emit the `sshd_config` watch only when `/etc/ssh` exists (or when `openssh` is installed). Use Omarchy-specific keys (for example `omarchy-identity`) so lines cannot exactly duplicate common CIS or STIG rules. Consider a base section as in upstream's `10-base-config.rules` (`-D`, and an explicit `-b` backlog instead of the kernel default of 64).

### Omarchy's own sudo and PAM changes are not watched

The file watches `/etc/sudoers` and `/etc/security/faillock.conf`. Omarchy writes its sudo policy to `/etc/sudoers.d/` instead: `install/config/increase-sudo-tries.sh`, `install/config/timezones.sh`, `install/config/sudoless-asdcontrol.sh`, and `bin/omarchy-sudo-passwordless`, which adds a `NOPASSWD` rule. PAM changes go to `/etc/pam.d/` (`install/config/increase-lockout-limit.sh`, `install/login/sddm.sh`, `bin/omarchy-setup-security-fingerprint`, `bin/omarchy-setup-security-fido2`). Arch's `sshd_config` includes `/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/*.conf`, which is also unwatched.

**Impact:** Most of the privilege-relevant configuration changes that happen on Omarchy would not be recorded, which does not match the stated purpose (sudoers and authentication files).

**Suggested change:** Add directory watches for `/etc/sudoers.d/` and `/etc/pam.d/`, and for `/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/` under the same guard as the `sshd_config` line.

**Rollout and target branch:** The script only runs from `install/config/all.sh` on fresh installs, and no migration is added, so existing installs never get the rules. The PR targets `dev`, whose last commit is from 2026-08-12. The repository's default branch is now `quattro`, where `install/config/all.sh` has a different structure. Maintainers may want to confirm the intended branch and whether existing installs should be covered.

**Optional test improvement:** `test/audit-rules-test.sh` greps 5 of the 12 lines from the generated file. In sandboxed mutation runs it still passed with a misspelled rule action (`alwayz,exit`), with the b32 `execve` rule removed, and with the whole enable, restart and load block deleted. It also calls the real `systemctl list-unit-files` (not stubbed), and its `sudo` stub runs any unrecognised command directly (`else "$@"`). Stubbing `systemctl`, making the `sudo` stub fail on unexpected commands, and asserting the enable call would let the test catch those cases.

---

## Review information

**Test scope:** Source review of the pinned head (`52ebdb1b`) and its base, plus the audit userspace (4.1.4 and 4.2.1), Arch packaging, systemd (v260.1 and v262), Linux kernel audit source, arch-install-scripts and the Omarchy ISO install scripts. One sandboxed run exercised the install script and the PR test with `sudo`, `systemctl` and `auditctl` stubbed, including the mutation cases above. No rules were loaded into a real kernel, and no real install or reboot was performed, so boot-time loading, the `/etc/ssh` failure and the performance or backlog cost of enabling auditing are source-derived, not observed.

**AI process:** Opus 5.5 Medium coordination and synthesis, independent Opus 5.5 Xhigh and GPT 6 Sol Xhigh technical assessments with targeted follow-up questions, Opus 5.5 Medium editorial check.
